header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are the integrating analyst of a code-safety review. Six departments have each committed `findings/<department>.json` and `report/<department>.md` on their own branch, and this worktree is the merge of all of them. You write two files and nothing else: `findings.json` and `SAFETY-REPORT.md`.

Read `REPORTING.md` in this worktree first: it states the finding format, the exact sections of the report, the count lines both summaries carry, and the certificate's wording. Read `target.json` for the tree under review and the SHA-256 the certificate states. Read every `findings/*.json` and every `report/*.md` before writing anything. When a `report-template` skill is available, load it: it owns how the report reads, while `REPORTING.md` owns what the examiner mechanically decides and wins wherever the two differ in form.

Ask the examiner which findings do not hold before you write the union:

    for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done

Every id it prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason. Dropping one silently fails the report.

`findings.json` is the union, deduplicated by `file` plus `line` plus `cwe`, keeping the entry whose `confidence` is higher. Copy each entry whole; do not rewrite a department's `snippet`, because the examiner compares it with the target's own text.

The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by the committed examiner, over the files the departments actually read. `## Scope and method` says that, names the departments that ran and the tools that ran, and states what was read rather than what exists. `## What was not covered` is not a formality: name the file kinds nobody opened, the classes of defect no department owns, the checks that did not run, and every dropped finding. Never write that the target is secure, safe or free of vulnerabilities — nothing this program did could support it, and the examiner refuses the claim.

Before you stop, run `node verify-safety-report.mjs --report`, fix every line it names, and commit everything. Work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured. Never write into the target tree, and never edit `verify-safety-report.mjs`, `target.json` or any department's committed files.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one is sampled across top-level entries, so it spans the tree instead of one subtree.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result instead returns 100 paths sampled across top-level entries, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

3: This worktree is the **report repository**. The code under review is the **target tree**, which is somewhere else on this host: `target.json` beside this file states its absolute path, the files it covers, and the SHA-256 the whole tree locks to.
4: 
5: The target is read-only for every session of this program. `verify-safety-report.mjs` re-hashes every locked file on every run, so a target a department edited fails the program instead of releasing a report about a tree that no longer exists.
6: 
7: ## This file and the skills
8: 
9: When the deployment mounts the code-safety knowledge pack, its `review-method`, `severity-and-evidence` and `report-template` skills own the craft: how to read a codebase, how to score a severity, what evidence has to name, and how the report reads. Follow them.
10: 
11: This file owns what `verify-safety-report.mjs` mechanically decides, and it is binding wherever the two differ in form. There is one such place and it is stated below: the counts each summary carries are written as `- <severity>: <count>` lines so the examiner can compare them with the union, which is the machine-readable form of the skill's "counts per severity".
12: 
13: ## What a department delivers
14: 
15: Two files, both committed on the department's own branch:
16: 
17: - `findings/<department>.json` — a JSON array of findings, `[]` when the department found nothing.
18: - `report/<department>.md` — the department's own prose: what it looked at, what it found, and what it did not reach.
19: 
20: Nothing else. Do not write `SAFETY-REPORT.md`, `findings.json`, `target.json` or `verify-safety-report.mjs`: the first two are the integration's, and the last two are the examiner.
21: 
22: ## The evidence rule
23: 
24: A finding without a file and a line is not a finding. Quote the exact line you cite; `verify-safety-report.mjs` compares your `snippet` with the target's own text at that line, ignoring only whitespace, and refuses the whole file when they differ.
25: 
26: Prefer three findings you have read the code for over twelve a pattern matched. `confidence` is what you actually know: `confirmed` when you read the sink, the source and the path between them; `likely` when the sink is dangerous and the source is plausibly attacker-controlled; `possible` when the pattern is there and the reachability is not established.
27: 
28: ## The finding
29: 
30: ```json
31: {
32:   "id": "secrets-cookie-secret",
33:   "cwe": "CWE-798",
34:   "owasp": "A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures",
35:   "severity": "high",
36:   "confidence": "confirmed",
37:   "title": "Session cookie secret is hard-coded in the committed configuration",
38:   "file": "config/env/all.js",
39:   "line": 8,
40:   "snippet": "cookieSecret: \"session_cookie_secret_key_here\",",
41:   "evidence": "The value is a literal in a committed file and is the secret express-session is configured with.",
42:   "impact": "Anyone with the repository can forge a session cookie and authenticate as any user.",
43:   "fix": "Read the secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.",
44:   "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html"]
45: }
46: ```
47: 
48: | Field | Rule |
49: | --- | --- |
50: | `id` | letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, unique across the whole program; prefix it with your department or use the pack's `SEC-<n>` numbering. |
51: | `cwe` | `CWE-<number>`. |
52: | `owasp` | the OWASP Top 10 category, named. |
53: | `severity` | `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low` or `info`. |
54: | `confidence` | `confirmed`, `likely` or `possible`. |
55: | `title` | one line a reader can act on. |
56: | `file` | path relative to the target root, exactly as `target.json` lists it. |
57: | `line` | 1-based line in that file. |
58: | `endLine` | optional last line when the finding spans several; `snippet` then quotes all of them. |
59: | `snippet` | the target's own text at those lines, verbatim. |
60: | `evidence` | why this line is the vulnerability, naming what you read. |
61: | `impact` | what an attacker gets. |
62: | `fix` | what to change. |
63: | `references` | array of URLs or identifiers; may be empty. |
64: 
65: ## Checking your own work before you commit
66: 
67: ```sh
68: node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/<department>.json
69: ```
70: 
71: That is the same command your goal is measured by. Run it, fix what it names, then commit everything — work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured.
72: 
73: ## What the integration delivers
74: 
75: The integration merges every department branch and then writes two files of its own.
76: 
77: `findings.json` is the union of every `findings/<department>.json`, deduplicated by `file` + `line` + `cwe`, keeping the entry with the higher `confidence`. Before writing it, ask the examiner which findings do not hold:
78: 
79: ```sh
80: for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done
81: ```
82: 
83: Every id that command prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason the examiner gave. Dropping one silently fails the report: `--report` refuses a union that omits an id no section discloses.
84: 
85: `SAFETY-REPORT.md` carries exactly these sections, in this order:
86: 
87: ```markdown
88: ## Résumé exécutif
89: 
90: <deux paragraphes en français : ce qui a été examiné, ce qui a été trouvé, ce que cela implique>
91: 
92: - critical: 0
93: - high: 0
94: - medium: 0
95: - low: 0
96: - info: 0
97: 
98: ## Executive summary
99: 
100: <the same in English>
101: 
102: - critical: 0
103: - high: 0
104: - medium: 0
105: - low: 0
106: - info: 0
107: 
108: ## Scope and method
109: 
110: <the target, its locked file count, which departments ran, which tools ran — the scanner, the advisory source — and which files were actually read>
111: 
112: ## Findings
113: 
114: ### critical
115: 
116: - `<id>` — <title> (`<file>:<line>`, <cwe>, <confidence>) — <impact, then fix>
117: 
118: ### high
119: 
120: ...
121: 
122: ## What was not covered
123: 
124: - <a department, a file kind, a class of vulnerability, or a check that did not run, and why>
125: - <every dropped finding id, with the examiner's reason>
126: 
127: ## Certificate
128: 
129: Verified findings: <count>
130: Target tree: <the sha256 from target.json>
131: 
132: <one sentence on what was checked mechanically: that every finding resolves to a real file and line in the locked tree, that every id is unique, and that no two findings share file, line and CWE>
133: 
134: This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".
135: ```
136: 
137: Both summary sections state a `- <severity>: <count>` line for all five severities, and the five counts must be the counts `findings.json` actually holds. Every finding id in `findings.json` is cited in `## Findings`. Every `<file>:<line>` written anywhere in the report must resolve in the target, so write a path you did not read as prose rather than as a citation.
138: 
139: The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by this examiner. Say so in `## Scope and method`. Never write that the target is secure, safe, or free of vulnerabilities: `verify-safety-report.mjs` refuses those claims, because nothing this program did could support one.
140: 
141: Check it before you commit:
142: 
143: ```sh
144: node verify-safety-report.mjs --report
145: ```

(End of file - total 145 lines)

<skill_instructions>
# The report layout

Every report has exactly these sections, in this order. Do not add marketing language, severity totals presented as a score out of ten, or a remediation timeline the review has no authority to commit the customer to.

- **`## Résumé exécutif`** — French. Counts per severity, the three most important findings by name and effect, what was and was not covered in one sentence each, and one paragraph on method.
- **`## Executive summary`** — the same content in English, for a mixed-language or non-French reader.
- **`## Scope and method`** — the repository, commit or tag reviewed, which directories or services were in scope, and a link to [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).
- **`## Findings`** — grouped by severity, critical first; one bullet per finding with its id, title, `file:line`, CWE, and confidence. Full detail (snippet, evidence, impact, fix) lives in the accompanying JSON per [severity-and-evidence](../severity-and-evidence/SKILL.md), not duplicated in prose here.
- **`## What was not covered`** — the [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md) not-covered list, specific to this engagement.
- **`## Certificate`** — what a mechanical verifier checked after the fact: every finding resolves to a real file and line in the reviewed commit, every id is unique, every CWE/OWASP id is a known identifier, and no two findings share file, line, and CWE. This certifies the report's internal consistency, not the completeness or correctness of the review's judgment.

## Filled example: a small Express app

```markdown
## Résumé exécutif

Cette revue a porté sur le code source de commande-api, une application Express.js
de gestion de commandes, au commit a1b2c3d. Elle a permis d'identifier 3 constats :
1 critique, 1 moyen et 1 faible. Les plus importants : (1) une injection SQL
critique dans la recherche de commande par identifiant (src/routes/orders.js:42),
permettant de lire ou modifier toute donnée accessible par l'utilisateur de base de
données de l'application ; (2) une fixation de session lors de la connexion
(src/routes/auth.js:58) ; (3) l'absence de l'en-tête HSTS (src/app.js:12). La revue
a couvert les points d'entrée HTTP, l'authentification et la gestion des sessions ;
elle n'a pas couvert l'infrastructure de déploiement ni les dépendances tierces
(voir « Ce qui n'a pas été couvert »). Méthode : lecture des points d'entrée,
suivi des données de la source jusqu'au point d'exécution, un constat par point
d'exécution, ligne exactement citée et niveau de confiance déclaré pour chacun.

## Executive summary

This review covered commande-api, an Express.js order-management application, at
commit a1b2c3d, and found 3 issues: 1 critical, 1 medium, 1 low. The most
important: (1) a critical SQL injection in order lookup by id
(src/routes/orders.js:42); (2) session fixation on login
(src/routes/auth.js:58); (3) a missing HSTS header (src/app.js:12). HTTP entry
points, authentication, and session handling were covered; deployment
infrastructure and third-party dependencies were not (see "What was not covered").

## Scope and method

Repository commande-api, commit a1b2c3d, `src/` only. Method: [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).

## Findings

### Critical
- SEC-001 — SQL injection in order lookup — `src/routes/orders.js:42` — CWE-89 — confirmed

### Medium
- SEC-002 — Session id not rotated after login (session fixation) — `src/routes/auth.js:58` — CWE-384 — likely

### Low
- SEC-003 — Missing Strict-Transport-Security header — `src/app.js:12` — CWE-319 — confirmed

## What was not covered

- `infra/` (Terraform, Dockerfiles) and CI/CD configuration.
- Third-party dependency advisories (separate engagement).
- Runtime configuration: actual deployed environment variables, WAF rules, and network topology.
- Native mobile or memory-safety classes of bug: this codebase has no native module.

## Certificate

Mechanically verified: 3/3 findings resolve to an existing line at commit a1b2c3d;
3/3 ids unique; 3/3 CWE and OWASP ids recognized; 0 findings share file, line, and
CWE. This certifies internal consistency only, not completeness of coverage.
```
</skill_instructions>
</skill_content>

1: #!/usr/bin/env node
2: // Mechanical examiner of a code-safety report. It is in the report
3: // repository's base commit, so no department can change what measures it.
4: //
5: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings <path>  one department's findings
6: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings <path> --list-invalid
7: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --report           the merged report
8: //
9: // `--findings` decides one findings file against the target tree. Adding
10: // `--list-invalid` turns the same decision into a report: the failing ids go to
11: // stdout, one per line, and the exit code is 0, which is how the integration
12: // learns which findings to drop and disclose.
13: //
14: // `--report` decides SAFETY-REPORT.md and findings.json together, including the
15: // disclosure rule: every id any `findings/<department>.json` carries and
16: // findings.json does not must be named under `## What was not covered`.
17: //
18: // Exit 0 only when every rule holds; otherwise every failure is printed to
19: // stderr, one per line, and the exit code is 1. Node built-ins only, because
20: // this runs in a worktree that installs nothing.
21: import { createHash } from 'node:crypto'
22: import { existsSync, readdirSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
23: import { basename, join, relative, resolve } from 'node:path'
24: 
25: /** Severities a finding may claim, most severe first. */
26: const SEVERITIES = ['critical', 'high', 'medium', 'low', 'info']
27: 
28: /** How sure a finding's author is that the cited code is exploitable as described. */
29: const CONFIDENCES = ['confirmed', 'likely', 'possible']
30: 
31: /** Sections SAFETY-REPORT.md carries, in this order. */
32: const SECTIONS = [
33:   '## Résumé exécutif',
34:   '## Executive summary',
35:   '## Scope and method',
36:   '## Findings',
37:   '## What was not covered',
38:   '## Certificate',
39: ]
40: 
41: /** The claim the certificate must make verbatim, and the only claim this review supports. */
42: const HONESTY = 'This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".'
43: 
44: /** Claims no coverage this review can state would support. */
45: const OVERCLAIMS = /\bno vulnerabilities\b|\bfree of vulnerabilities\b|\b(?:is|are|was|were) secure\b|\bsafe to deploy\b|\bproven secure\b|\bfully audited\b/i
46: 
47: /** Text a report still carrying its template is refused for. */
48: const PLACEHOLDER = /\bTODO\b|\bTBD\b|\bFIXME\b|lorem ipsum|<placeholder>|PLACEHOLDER/i
49: 
50: /** String fields every finding states in prose. */
51: const PROSE_FIELDS = ['title', 'evidence', 'impact', 'fix']
52: 
53: /** How a file's text is compared with a finding's quoted snippet. */
54: const normalize = (text) => text.replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim()
55: 
56: /** Lowercase hex SHA-256 of one buffer or string. */
57: const sha256 = (content) => createHash('sha256').update(content).digest('hex')
58: 
59: /**
60:  * Every file under one directory, relative and sorted, skipping the excluded names.
61:  * @param {string} root directory to walk
62:  * @param {string[]} exclude directory basenames never descended into
63:  * @returns {string[]} relative POSIX-ish paths, sorted
64:  */
65: function walk(root, exclude) {
66:   const found = []
67:   const descend = (directory) => {
68:     for (const entry of readdirSync(directory, { withFileTypes: true }).sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name))) {
69:       const path = join(directory, entry.name)
70:       if (entry.isDirectory()) {
71:         if (!exclude.includes(entry.name)) descend(path)
72:       } else if (entry.isFile()) found.push(relative(root, path))
73:     }
74:   }
75:   descend(root)
76:   return found.sort()
77: }
78: 
79: /** One target tree as the lock and the verifier both read it: the files, their digests, and their text. */
80: class Target {
81:   /**
82:    * @param {string} reportRoot the report repository the lock is committed in
83:    * @param {string[]} failures collector every rule appends to
84:    */
85:   constructor(reportRoot, failures) {
86:     this.failures = failures
87:     this.root = undefined
88:     this.files = new Map()
89:     this.lines = new Map()
90:     const lockPath = join(reportRoot, 'target.json')
91:     if (!existsSync(lockPath)) {
92:       failures.push('target.json is missing from this worktree; the base commit carries the lock of the tree under review')
93:       return
94:     }
95:     const lock = JSON.parse(readFileSync(lockPath, 'utf8'))
96:     this.root = lock.root
97:     this.exclude = lock.exclude ?? []
98:     this.digest = lock.sha256
99:     for (const [path, hash] of Object.entries(lock.files)) this.files.set(path, hash)
100:     this.checkTree()
101:   }
102: 
103:   /**
104:    * Refuse a target that changed since the base commit locked it: a finding
105:    * cites a line of the tree this program was asked to review, and a tree a
106:    * department edited is no longer that tree.
107:    */
108:   checkTree() {
109:     if (!existsSync(this.root)) {
110:       this.failures.push(`the target tree ${this.root} is not on this host, so no citation can be resolved`)
111:       this.root = undefined
112:       return
113:     }
114:     const present = walk(this.root, this.exclude)
115:     for (const path of present) {
116:       if (!this.files.has(path)) this.failures.push(`the target tree gained ${path} since the base commit locked it`)
117:     }
118:     for (const [path, hash] of this.files) {
119:       if (!present.includes(path)) {
120:         this.failures.push(`the target tree lost ${path} since the base commit locked it`)
121:         continue
122:       }
123:       if (sha256(readFileSync(join(this.root, path))) !== hash) {
124:         this.failures.push(`the target tree's ${path} changed since the base commit locked it; the target is read-only for this program`)
125:       }
126:     }
127:   }
128: 
129:   /**
130:    * The lines of one target file.
131:    * @param {string} path path relative to the target root
132:    * @returns {string[] | undefined} the file's lines, or undefined when it is not in the locked tree
133:    */
134:   linesOf(path) {
135:     if (this.root === undefined || !this.files.has(path)) return undefined
136:     if (!this.lines.has(path)) this.lines.set(path, readFileSync(join(this.root, path), 'utf8').split('\n'))
137:     return this.lines.get(path)
138:   }
139: 
140:   /**
141:    * Whether one `file:line` citation resolves in the locked tree.
142:    * @param {string} path path relative to the target root
143:    * @param {number} line 1-based line number
144:    * @returns {boolean} whether the file is under review and holds that line
145:    */
146:   resolves(path, line) {
147:     const lines = this.linesOf(path)
148:     return lines !== undefined && Number.isInteger(line) && line >= 1 && line <= lines.length
149:   }
150: }
151: 
152: /**
153:  * Decide one finding against the target tree.
154:  * @param {unknown} finding one entry of a findings file
155:  * @param {number} index its position, named when the entry has no usable id
156:  * @param {Target} target the locked tree the finding cites
157:  * @param {Set<string>} seen ids already used in this file
158:  * @returns {string[]} every rule this finding broke, empty when it holds
159:  */
160: function checkFinding(finding, index, target, seen) {
161:   const failures = []
162:   if (finding === null || typeof finding !== 'object' || Array.isArray(finding)) {
163:     return [`finding #${index + 1} is not a JSON object`]
164:   }
165:   const id = finding.id
166:   const name = typeof id === 'string' && id !== '' ? id : `#${index + 1}`
167:   const fail = (rule) => void failures.push(`${name}: ${rule}`)
168:   // Letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`: wide enough for both the `SEC-001`
169:   // numbering the knowledge pack's schema uses and a department-prefixed name.
170:   if (typeof id !== 'string' || !/^[A-Za-z0-9][\w.-]*$/.test(id)) fail('id must be letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores')
171:   else if (seen.has(id)) fail('id is used twice in this file')
172:   else seen.add(id)
173:   if (typeof finding.cwe !== 'string' || !/^CWE-\d+$/.test(finding.cwe)) fail('cwe must match CWE-<number>')
174:   if (typeof finding.owasp !== 'string' || finding.owasp.trim() === '') fail('owasp must name the category')
175:   if (!SEVERITIES.includes(finding.severity)) fail(`severity must be one of ${SEVERITIES.join(', ')}`)
176:   if (!CONFIDENCES.includes(finding.confidence)) fail(`confidence must be one of ${CONFIDENCES.join(', ')}`)
177:   for (const field of PROSE_FIELDS) {
178:     if (typeof finding[field] !== 'string' || finding[field].trim() === '') fail(`${field} must be a non-empty string`)
179:   }
180:   if (!Array.isArray(finding.references) || finding.references.some(reference => typeof reference !== 'string')) {
181:     fail('references must be an array of strings')
182:   }
183:   const { file, line, endLine, snippet } = finding
184:   if (typeof file !== 'string' || file === '' || file.startsWith('/') || file.split('/').includes('..')) {
185:     fail('file must be a path relative to the target root')
186:     return failures
187:   }
188:   const lines = target.linesOf(file)

"impact": "An attacker can send a JSON login request with userName set to an operator object (e.g. {\"$ne\": null}) to make the query match an arbitrary existing user document instead of a specific named account, enabling user enumeration and altering the intended authentication query logic.",

"fix": "Reject non-string values for userName/password before querying (e.g. if (typeof userName !== 'string') return callback(...)), or cast with String(userName) and validate against an expected format before it reaches findOne().",

"title": "No rate limiting or lockout on the login endpoint",

"evidence": "package.json's dependency list (read in full) contains no rate-limiting package (no express-rate-limit, express-brute, or similar), and a repository-wide search for `rate-limit`/`rateLimit` returns no matches. app/routes/session.js's handleLoginRequest (lines 53-119, read in full) calls userDAO.validateLogin directly on every POST with no counter, delay, CAPTCHA or lockout of any kind, and the route at this line has no limiting middleware placed before handleLoginRequest.",

"impact": "An attacker can submit unlimited password guesses per username with no throttling, making online brute-force or credential-stuffing against every account (including the hard-coded admin account seeded by artifacts/db-reset.js) practical.",
"fix": "Add a rate limiter (express-rate-limit or equivalent) keyed by IP and by submitted username in front of POST /login, and lock out or delay after a small number of failures.",
"title": "/learn redirects to an attacker-controlled URL taken directly from the query string",

"evidence": "req.query.url, fully attacker-controlled, is passed straight to res.redirect() with no allow-list, host check, or relative-path enforcement of any kind on this line or anywhere earlier in the handler.",

"impact": "An attacker sends a logged-in victim a link to https://<app-host>/learn?url=https://evil.example/phish; the app itself performs the redirect from a trusted domain, which is effective for phishing and for bypassing URL-reputation filters that trust the NodeGoat host.",
"fix": "Validate req.query.url against an allow-list of known learning-resource hosts (or store the target server-side and redirect by an opaque id) before calling res.redirect().",
"title": "Global error handler renders the raw caught Error object into the response",

"evidence": "The errorHandler (app/routes/error.js, read in full) logs err.message and err.stack to the server console (lines 7-8) and then, separately, passes the entire `err` object as the `error` template variable at line 11 into app/views/error-template.html, whose only body content is `
{{error}}` (line 11 of that file). server.js line 137 sets swig.setDefaults({ autoescape: false }) globally, so whatever `err`'s string form contains is written into the HTML response unescaped. Any handler in the app that calls `next(err)` with a raw MongoDB or validation error (e.g. app/routes/session.js:100 `return next(err)`, app/routes/profile.js:21/93, app/routes/contributions.js:18/67) reaches this same sink.",

"impact": "A client that triggers any unhandled error (a malformed request, a database hiccup) receives the internal error message/type reflected back verbatim, which can reveal internal logic, library names and versions, or partial query content useful for further attacks, and can carry attacker input back unescaped.",
"fix": "Log the full error server-side only, generate a correlation id, and render a generic message plus that id to the client instead of the error object itself.",
"title": "Configuration silently falls back to the development environment, which injects a livereload script tag into every page",

"evidence": "docker-compose.yml line 7 declares `NODE_ENV:` with no value for the `web` service, which sets the container's NODE_ENV to an empty string; an empty string is falsy in JavaScript, so `process.env.NODE_ENV || \"development\"` on this line evaluates to \"development\" for exactly the deployment path package.json's own `start-infra` script (`docker-compose up`) drives. config/env/development.js is then merged in (config/config.js line 10) and its `environmentalScripts` array (development.js lines 9-13) injects `<script>document.write(\"<script src='http://\" + (location.host||\"localhost\").split(\":\")[0] + \":35729/livereload.js'></\" + \"script>\");</script>` into every rendered page (every view template passes `environmentalScripts` through, e.g. app/routes/session.js:49/88/97/134/271).",

"impact": "The docker-compose deployment path silently runs with development settings, including a script that makes every page load fetch and execute a script from a livereload server at a location derived from the request's own Host header, and exposes the OWASP ZAP API key/host from development.js in the merged config object logged to stdout by config/config.js lines 12-13.",
"fix": "Fail startup when NODE_ENV is unset/empty instead of defaulting to \"development\", and set NODE_ENV=production explicitly in docker-compose.yml's environment block for the web service.",
"title": "Server only ever listens over plain HTTP; the HTTPS listener is fully commented out",

"evidence": "server.js imports `http` (line 12) and calls only `http.createServer(app).listen(port, ...)` at these lines. The alternative `https.createServer(httpsOptions, app).listen(...)` block (lines 149-155) and the `fs`/`https`/`path`/`httpsOptions` setup that would load artifacts/cert/server.key and artifacts/cert/server.crt (lines 18-28) are both commented out, even though the certificate files themselves are committed at artifacts/cert/server.crt and artifacts/cert/server.key.",

"impact": "All traffic, including login credentials (app/routes/session.js handleLoginRequest posts userName/password in the body) and the session cookie, is transmitted in cleartext and can be read or modified by anyone on the network path.",

"fix": "Uncomment the https.createServer block and the certificate loading above it, and terminate TLS at the application (or a TLS-terminating proxy in front of it) rather than serving over http.createServer.",

32: ## Executive summary
33: 
34: This review covered NodeGoat (`/root/targets/NodeGoat`, 111 files locked by
35: `target.json`), a deliberately vulnerable OWASP training application, scoped to
36: authentication, session handling, and authorization. Eight findings were
37: confirmed, all at `confirmed` confidence: 4 high severity and 4 medium, none
38: critical or low. The most significant: (1) login
39: (`app/routes/session.js:116`) never regenerates the session id after
40: authentication, enabling session fixation; (2) `POST /benefits`
41: (`app/routes/index.js:56`) is guarded only by a login check, not the admin role
42: check the code's own commented-out fix shows was intended, letting any logged-in
43: user rewrite any other user's benefits start date; (3) passwords are stored and
44: compared in plaintext (`app/data/user-dao.js:61`) instead of with the bcrypt
45: dependency already present in the project. Every route file under
46: `app/routes`, every DAO under `app/data`, and the session configuration in
47: `server.js` were read; injection classes, secret management, and third-party
48: dependency advisories were out of scope for this department and are not
49: covered here. Method: every HTTP entry point registered in
50: `app/routes/index.js` was enumerated, each route's middleware chain was traced,
51: one finding per broken control, the exact line quoted, and a confidence level
52: stated for each. `semgrep` (v1.177.0, the repository's local rule pack plus
53: `p/owasp-top-ten`) was run first and every hit was used as a place to read, not
54: reported directly as a finding.
55: 
56: - critical: 0
57: - high: 4
58: - medium: 4
59: - low: 0
60: - info: 0
61: 
62: ## Scope and method
63: 
64: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (locked by `target.json`, sha256
65: `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`), read-only,
66: 111 files. In scope for this department: `server.js` (session middleware and
67: app bootstrap), every route module under `app/routes/` (`index.js`,
68: `session.js`, `profile.js`, `benefits.js`, `contributions.js`,
69: `allocations.js`, `memos.js`, `research.js`, `tutorial.js`, `error.js`), the
70: DAO layer under `app/data/` insofar as it implements authentication or
71: authorization decisions (`user-dao.js`, `benefits-dao.js`,
72: `allocations-dao.js`), and `config/env/all.js` for session secret and cookie
73: configuration. The corresponding view templates (`app/views/benefits.html`,
74: `app/views/allocations.html`) were read to confirm what data each route
75: actually exposes or writes.
76: 
77: Method: [review-method](../../../../data/knowledge/code-safety/review-method/SKILL.md)
78: — entry points enumerated first from `app/routes/index.js`'s route table, then
79: each route's middleware chain traced from registration through to its handler
80: and DAO call, one finding per broken control, exact line quoted verbatim, and
81: confidence recorded as `confirmed` only when the full source-to-sink path
82: (including the surrounding guards) was read.
83: 
84: `semgrep` v1.177.0 was run with the repository's local rule pack
85: (`examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/program-code-safety/semgrep`) plus the
86: registry pack `p/owasp-top-ten`, `--metrics off --json`, over the full target
87: tree (29 findings across 113 rules). Every hit was treated as a place to read,
88: never as a finding on its own; the `javascript.express.security.audit.express-cookie-settings`
89: hits at `server.js:78` and the hardcoded-secret hit at `config/env/all.js:8`
90: were the ones most relevant to this department and are reflected in the
91: findings below (or noted as out of scope, respectively — the hardcoded cookie
92: secret is reported by the secrets department, not duplicated here).
93: 
94: ## Findings
95: 
96: ### High
97: 
98: - `access-session-fixation-login` — Session id is not regenerated after successful login (session fixation) — `app/routes/session.js:116` — CWE-384 — confirmed
99: - `access-benefits-post-missing-admin-check` — POST /benefits lets any logged-in user change any other user's benefit start date — `app/routes/index.js:56` — CWE-862 — confirmed
100: - `access-csrf-missing-profile` — No CSRF protection on state-changing routes; csurf is a dependency but never mounted — `app/routes/index.js:48` — CWE-352 — confirmed
101: - `access-plaintext-password-storage-comparison` — Passwords are stored and compared in plaintext instead of hashed — `app/data/user-dao.js:61` — CWE-256 — confirmed
102: 
103: ### Medium
104: 
105: - `access-benefits-get-missing-admin-check` — GET /benefits exposes the admin benefits roster to any logged-in user, not just admins — `app/routes/index.js:55` — CWE-862 — confirmed
106: - `access-allocations-idor` — GET /allocations/:userId returns any user's stock allocations by URL parameter, not the caller's own — `app/routes/index.js:63` — CWE-639 — confirmed
107: - `access-login-no-rate-limit` — POST /login has no rate limit, lockout or delay — `app/routes/index.js:34` — CWE-307 — confirmed
108: - `access-session-cookie-flags-missing` — Session cookie is configured with no httpOnly, secure or maxAge settings — `server.js:78` — CWE-614 — confirmed
109: 
110: ## What was not covered
111: 
112: - Injection classes (NoSQL `$where` injection in `app/data/allocations-dao.js:73/78`, `eval()` on request input in `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`, open redirect in `app/routes/index.js:72`, SSRF in `app/routes/research.js`): flagged by `semgrep` and read while tracing routes, but they belong to the injection department and are not scored here.
113: - Secrets and cryptography (`cookieSecret` and `cryptoKey` hardcoded in `config/env/all.js:8-9`, also present in `config/env/development.js:6` and `config/env/test.js:6`): read and confirmed present, but reported by the secrets/data departments, not duplicated here.
114: - The dependency tree (`package.json`, `package-lock.json`) was read only to confirm the absence of a rate-limiting package and the presence of the unused `csurf`/`bcrypt-nodejs`/`helmet` packages; a full advisory sweep is the dependencies department's job.
115: - `app/routes/tutorial.js` and its templates were read and confirmed to require no session (they are static OWASP-lesson pages with no data access), so no authorization finding was raised there.
116: - `app/routes/memos.js` and `app/routes/research.js`/`contributions.js` were read for their session/authorization handling only; their DAOs' query construction and template escaping were not analyzed beyond that (out of department).
117: - MFA: NodeGoat implements no multi-factor authentication anywhere in the reviewed routes, so there is no MFA-skip path to evaluate; this is a design gap rather than a specific line-level finding and is noted here rather than filed.
118: - Runtime behavior — the actual deployed `NODE_ENV`, whether HTTPS termination happens at a reverse proxy in front of the app, and any WAF/rate-limiting applied outside this repository — cannot be confirmed by a static read and was not assumed.
119: - Timing-attack exploitability of the `fromDB === fromUser` comparison in `app/data/user-dao.js:61` was not measured; the finding is scored on the plaintext-storage impact, which was confirmed, not on a measured timing side channel.
120: 
121: ## Certificate
122: 
123: Verified findings: 8
124: Target tree: 78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3
125: 
126: `node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/access.json` mechanically confirmed that all 8 findings resolve to an existing file and line in the locked target tree with a matching snippet, that all 8 ids are unique, and that no two findings share file, line and CWE.
127: 
128: This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".

(End of file - total 128 lines)

1: # Data department — sensitive data exposure, logging and cryptography
2: 
3: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked in `target.json`, sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`). This review is a static read by a language model, grounded by Semgrep and by the mechanical examiner `verify-safety-report.mjs`; it does not run the application.
4: 
5: ## Method
6: 
7: `semgrep --version` reported `1.177.0`, so it was run over the target with `p/owasp-top-ten` plus the local `dsh-*` rule pack, `--metrics off --json`, from the target root. The registry pack was reachable (29 findings, 113 rules run across 72 git-tracked files). Every Semgrep hit was read in context and treated as a lead, never as a finding on its own — several hits (the plaintext-HTTP links inside `app/views/tutorial/*.html`, the GitHub Actions mutable-tag warnings) were read and dropped because they are documentation content or CI supply-chain noise outside this department's scope, not data exposure in the running application.
8: 
9: Starting from the entry points (`server.js`, `app/routes/*.js`), sensitive values were traced forward: the login/signup password from `app/routes/session.js` into `app/data/user-dao.js`; the profile fields (ssn, dob, bankAcc, bankRouting) from `app/routes/profile.js` into `app/data/profile-dao.js`; the process config (`config/config.js`, `config/env/*.js`) from require-time through to its `console.log`; and the error object from `app/routes/error.js` into its template. Files actually opened and read line-by-line: `server.js`, `config/config.js`, `config/env/{all,development,production,test}.js`, `app/routes/{index,session,profile,error,benefits,contributions,memos,research}.js`, `app/data/{user,profile,allocations,benefits,contributions,memos,research}-dao.js`, `app/views/{error-template,dashboard,profile,benefits}.html`, `artifacts/db-reset.js`, `docker-compose.yml`, `Dockerfile`.
10: 
11: ## Findings
12: 
13: Six findings, all with a confirmed or explicitly `likely` confidence level; each is filed in `findings/data.json` with the exact cited line and a verbatim snippet checked against the locked target tree.
14: 
15: ### High-level summary
16: 
17: | id | severity | confidence | CWE | what leaves/rests where |
18: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
19: | data-001 | high | confirmed | CWE-532 | `cookieSecret` and `cryptoKey` printed to stdout on every boot |
20: | data-002 | critical | confirmed | CWE-256 | passwords stored and compared as plaintext |
21: | data-003 | high | confirmed | CWE-312 | SSN/DOB/bank account/bank routing stored as plaintext |
22: | data-004 | high | confirmed | CWE-319 | the whole app, including credentials and the session cookie, is served over plain HTTP |
23: | data-005 | medium | confirmed | CWE-532 | seed script logs every account's plaintext password on every container start |
24: | data-006 | medium | likely | CWE-209 | raw error object rendered to the client with no sanitization |
25: 
26: Full detail, including the exact evidence chain (source → intermediate → sink) for each, is in `findings/data.json`.
27: 
28: ### Notable corroboration
29: 
30: - `app/data/user-dao.js:1` requires `bcrypt-nodejs` and lines 27-30 contain the correct `bcrypt.hashSync` fix, commented out — the developer intent (and the deliberate vulnerability) is explicit, not inferred.
31: - `app/data/profile-dao.js:15-40` contains a complete, commented-out AES-encryption implementation for `ssn`/`dob` using `crypto.createCipheriv`/`createDecipheriv` with a fresh IV per call — again, the fix exists in the file and is simply disabled.
32: - `docker-compose.yml` starts the `mongo` service (lines 13-17) with no authentication configured at all, which raises the reachability of data-002 and data-003: the plaintext passwords and PII sit behind no database credential in the shipped deployment.
33: - `app/views/tutorial/a6.html` (the app's own built-in lesson content) documents both the plaintext-HTTP and plaintext-PII-storage issues as the intended teaching vulnerabilities, which is independent confirmation that data-003 and data-004 are the application's known, intentional weaknesses rather than an incidental misreading of dead code.
34: 
35: ## What was not covered
36: 
37: - **Session cookie flags** (`secure`, `httpOnly`, default cookie name) at `server.js:78-102` were read and are indeed weak, but are left to the `access`/`platform` departments whose skill scope names cookie flags explicitly; reporting them again here would just be the same lines under a different department.
38: - **`app/routes/index.js:70-73`** (open redirect) and **`app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`** (`eval` on request input) and the **`$where` NoSQL injection** in `app/data/allocations-dao.js:73-78` were all seen (several via Semgrep) and read, but they are injection/access-control findings, not data-exposure findings, and are left to the `injection` department.
39: - **`config/env/development.js:6` and `config/env/test.js:6`** hardcode a ZAP API key (`zapApiKey`). It was read and is a committed credential, but it authenticates only a local OWASP ZAP scanning proxy used in this project's own test tooling, not a production system; it is left to the `secrets` department to decide whether it merits a finding.
40: - **`config/env/all.js:8`** (`cookieSecret`) and **`:9`** (`cryptoKey`) as hardcoded-secret findings in their own right are left to the `secrets` department; this report instead follows those same two values forward to where they leave the system in cleartext (data-001).
41: - The rest of the 111-file tree — `.github/workflows/*`, `Gruntfile.js`, `package.json`/`package-lock.json`, the `app/assets/vendor/*` third-party JS/CSS bundles, and the Cypress/e2e fixtures under `test/e2e/` — was scanned by Semgrep and spot-checked, but not read line-by-line, since nothing there handles sensitive application data.
42: - No dynamic testing was performed: this review cannot confirm what a running instance actually writes to a real log aggregator, what a production `NODE_ENV` config file would contain (this repository's own `config/env/production.js` is empty, `module.exports = {}`, so production secret handling is not defined in this tree at all), or whether any WAF/proxy in front of a real deployment mitigates the plaintext-HTTP finding.
43: - Timing side channels, memory-safety issues in native/compiled dependencies, and the security of third-party npm packages themselves (only their *use* of sensitive data was in scope here) were not checked; that belongs to the `dependencies` department.

(End of file - total 43 lines)
</content>

| data-001 | high | confirmed | CWE-532 | `cookieSecret` and `cryptoKey` printed to stdout on every boot |
| data-002 | critical | confirmed | CWE-256 | passwords stored and compared as plaintext |
| data-003 | high | confirmed | CWE-312 | SSN/DOB/bank account/bank routing stored as plaintext |

- **`config/env/development.js:6` and `config/env/test.js:6`** hardcode a ZAP API key (`zapApiKey`). It was read and is a committed credential, but it authenticates only a local OWASP ZAP scanning proxy used in this project's own test tooling, not a production system; it is left to the `secrets` department to decide whether it merits a finding.

- **`config/env/all.js:8`** (`cookieSecret`) and **`:9`** (`cryptoKey`) as hardcoded-secret findings in their own right are left to the `secrets` department; this report instead follows those same two values forward to where they leave the system in cleartext (data-001).

- The rest of the 111-file tree — `.github/workflows/*`, `Gruntfile.js`, `package.json`/`package-lock.json`, the `app/assets/vendor/*` third-party JS/CSS bundles, and the Cypress/e2e fixtures under `test/e2e/` — was scanned by Semgrep and spot-checked, but not read line-by-line, since nothing there handles sensitive application data.

- No dynamic testing was performed: this review cannot confirm what a running instance actually writes to a real log aggregator, what a production `NODE_ENV` config file would contain (this repository's own `config/env/production.js` is empty, `module.exports = {}`, so production secret handling is not defined in this tree at all), or whether any WAF/proxy in front of a real deployment mitigates the plaintext-HTTP finding.

- Timing side channels, memory-safety issues in native/compiled dependencies, and the security of third-party npm packages themselves (only their *use* of sensitive data was in scope here) were not checked; that belongs to the `dependencies` department.

1: # Injection and traversal — NodeGoat
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked in `target.json`, sha256
6: `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`). The tree
7: was read only; no file in it was modified.
8: 
9: `semgrep --version` reported `1.177.0`. It was run once as:
10: 
11: ```
12: semgrep --config <local rule file> --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json /root/targets/NodeGoat
13: ```
14: 
15: The registry pack (`p/owasp-top-ten`) was reachable, so both the local rules
16: and the registry pack ran together: 113 rules over 72 git-tracked files, 29
17: raw hits. Every hit was treated as a lead to go read, never as a finding on
18: its own, per the department's instructions. Semgrep pointed at the `$where`
19: use in `app/data/allocations-dao.js`, the `eval()` calls in
20: `app/routes/contributions.js`, and the open redirect in `app/routes/index.js`;
21: the rest of its hits (mutable GitHub Actions tags, plaintext HTTP links in
22: tutorial pages, missing cookie flags, a hardcoded session secret) belong to
23: other departments (dependencies/platform/secrets) and are not repeated here.
24: 
25: Beyond the semgrep hits, every route handler under `app/routes/*.js`, every
26: DAO under `app/data/*.js`, `server.js`, and the templates the route handlers
27: render (`app/views/*.html`) were read end to end, tracing each
28: request-derived value (`req.query`, `req.body`, `req.session`, `req.params`)
29: forward to its sink. `config/*.js` and `Gruntfile.js` were read to rule out
30: command injection and template-string secrets reaching a shell; no
31: `child_process`/`exec`/`spawn` call in the runtime app (as opposed to the
32: build tooling and Cypress test harness) takes request data.
33: 
34: ## What was found
35: 
36: Seven findings, all `confirmed` — for each, the tainted source, every
37: intermediate function, and the sink were read, with no sanitizer or guard in
38: between:
39: 
40: - **Critical** — `eval()` on the three contribution-percentage fields
41:   (`app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`), CWE-95. Full server-side code
42:   execution from a POST body.
43: - **High** — NoSQL `$where` injection in the allocations threshold filter
44:   (`app/data/allocations-dao.js:77-79`), CWE-943; the query parameter reaches
45:   a JavaScript-evaluated `$where` clause unescaped.
46: - **High** — SSRF in the stock research lookup (`app/routes/research.js:15-16`),
47:   CWE-918; the outbound request's full URL, including host, is taken from the
48:   query string.
49: - **High** — stored XSS in shared memos (`app/views/memos.html:31`), CWE-79;
50:   compounded by swig's `autoescape: false` in `server.js:137`.
51: - **High** — reflected/stored XSS on the profile update error page
52:   (`app/views/profile.html:41`), CWE-79; a field literally named
53:   `firstNameSafeString` performs no encoding.
54: - **High** — NoSQL operator injection in the login query
55:   (`app/data/user-dao.js:91-93`), CWE-943; `req.body.userName` can be a JSON
56:   object because `bodyParser.json()` is registered, and it reaches
57:   `findOne()` unchecked.
58: - **Medium** — open redirect on `/learn` (`app/routes/index.js:72`), CWE-601;
59:   the code comment above the line calls this out as intentional.
60: 
61: Full detail, evidence, impact and fix for each is in `findings/injection.json`.
62: 
63: ## What was not covered
64: 
65: - `app/assets/**` (vendored jQuery, Bootstrap, morris.js, raphael, html5shiv)
66:   was not read line by line: it is unmodified third-party client-side code,
67:   out of scope for a source review of this application's own request
68:   handling, and any vulnerability in it is a dependency question, not an
69:   injection finding in NodeGoat's own code.
70: - `test/e2e/**` and `test/security/**` were not traced as attacker-reachable
71:   surface: they are the project's own Cypress/OWASP-ZAP test harness, not
72:   code that runs in production, though `test/e2e/support/commands.js:30`
73:   does call `cy.exec("npm run db:seed", ...)` with a fixed string — this is a
74:   test-fixture concern, not a finding here.
75: - `Gruntfile.js`'s `exec(...)` call (line 165) is a build-time task runner
76:   invocation with no request-derived input; it was read and excluded as a
77:   finding rather than left unchecked.
78: - ReDoS (the intentionally vulnerable `bankRouting` regex in
79:   `app/routes/profile.js:59`) and the CSRF/cookie/session issues visible in
80:   `server.js` were noted while reading but belong to other departments'
81:   mandates (platform, access) and are not reported here to avoid duplicate
82:   findings across departments.
83: - No dynamic testing (fuzzing, running the app, sending the crafted payloads
84:   described in each finding's `impact` field) was performed; every finding
85:   here is a static read of the source, not an observed exploit.
86: - Template injection proper (a template *string* built from request data)
87:   was checked for and not found: `res.render()` is always called with a
88:   fixed template name from a small server-side list (`app/routes/tutorial.js`
89:   is the only place a template name is built from a loop variable, and that
90:   variable is a fixed array of literals, never request input).

(End of file - total 90 lines)
</content>

30: ## Executive summary
31: 
32: This review covered the "platform" domain (security headers, CORS, cookies, error
33: handling, rate limiting, debug settings) of NodeGoat, an Express.js/MongoDB
34: application, in the read-only tree `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked by
35: `target.json`). The analysis began with a full read of `server.js`, the entry
36: point, then traced the actual middleware order and effective configuration rather
37: than the intent of commented-out code. It produced 10 findings, all confirmed by
38: direct reading: 6 high severity, 3 medium, 1 low, none critical or informational.
39: The three most important: (1) the express-session secret is a hard-coded literal
40: committed to the repository (`config/env/all.js:8`), letting anyone forge a valid
41: session; (2) every security-header middleware (helmet, CSP, X-Frame-Options, HSTS,
42: MIME-sniffing protection) is entirely commented out in `server.js:38-65`, so no
43: response carries any of it; (3) CSRF protection is likewise commented out
44: (`server.js:104-113`) even though the HTML forms still submit a `_csrf` token that
45: is never checked. `semgrep` (version 1.177.0, the program's local rule pack plus
46: `p/owasp-top-ten`, registry reachable) was used to find places to read, never as
47: proof by itself; every finding cites code actually read. The review did not cover
48: pure application-layer security (injection, IDOR, per-route authorization), third-
49: party dependency advisories, or actual production runtime behavior beyond what the
50: source supports inferring.
51: 
52: - critical: 0
53: - high: 6
54: - medium: 3
55: - low: 1
56: - info: 0
57: 
58: ## Scope and method
59: 
60: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (OWASP NodeGoat, the tree locked by `target.json`
61: next to `REPORTING.md`, sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`),
62: 111 files, read-only. In scope for this department: `server.js` (the entry point,
63: read end to end first), `config/config.js` and `config/env/*.js`, `app/routes/*.js`
64: (mounting order and per-route middleware), `app/routes/error.js` and
65: `app/views/error-template.html` (error handling), `app/routes/session.js`
66: (cookies, login), `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml` (deployment defaults), and
67: `package.json`/`package-lock.json` (which security middleware is a declared
68: dependency versus actually mounted).
69: 
70: Method: [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md) — entry point first, then trace
71: each attacker-reachable input or configuration value to its sink, one finding per
72: sink, exact line quoted, confidence stated per finding rather than assumed.
73: `semgrep --version` reported `1.177.0`; `semgrep --config <local pack> --config
74: p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json` was then run over the target (the registry
75: pack downloaded successfully, so it was kept alongside the local rules) and its 29
76: hits were read and triaged as leads, not findings — several confirmed the manual
77: reading (the express-cookie-settings rules on `server.js:78`, the hard-coded-secret
78: rule on `config/env/*.js`), the rest (GitHub Actions mutable tags, `eval()` in
79: `app/routes/contributions.js`, the open-redirect rule) were outside this
80: department's remit or already read and reported here.
81: 
82: ## Findings
83: 
84: ### High
85: 
86: - `platform-hardcoded-cookie-secret` — express-session secret is a hard-coded literal committed to the repository — `config/env/all.js:8` — CWE-798 — confirmed
87: - `platform-missing-security-headers` — Helmet and every security-header middleware is commented out, so no response carries them — `server.js:38-65` — CWE-693 — confirmed
88: - `platform-session-cookie-not-secure` — Session cookie is never marked Secure, and the server only listens on plain HTTP — `server.js:78-102` — CWE-614 — confirmed
89: - `platform-csrf-protection-disabled` — CSRF middleware is commented out even though every state-changing form still submits a `_csrf` token — `server.js:104-113` — CWE-352 — confirmed
90: - `platform-missing-rate-limit-login` — No rate limiting or lockout on the login endpoint — `app/routes/index.js:34` — CWE-307 — confirmed
91: - `platform-http-only-no-tls` — Server only ever listens over plain HTTP; the HTTPS listener is fully commented out — `server.js:144-147` — CWE-319 — confirmed
92: 
93: ### Medium
94: 
95: - `platform-open-redirect-learn` — `/learn` redirects to an attacker-controlled URL taken directly from the query string — `app/routes/index.js:70-73` — CWE-601 — confirmed
96: - `platform-error-handler-discloses-error-object` — Global error handler renders the raw caught Error object into the response — `app/routes/error.js:10-12` — CWE-209 — confirmed
97: - `platform-default-development-config` — Configuration silently falls back to the development environment, which injects a livereload script tag into every page — `config/config.js:5` — CWE-1188 — confirmed
98: 
99: ### Low
100: 
101: - `platform-session-cookie-default-name` — Session cookie keeps the express-session default name, fingerprinting the framework — `server.js:78-102` — CWE-200 — confirmed
102: 
103: ## What was not covered
104: 
105: - Application-layer authorization and injection classes (NoSQL/eval injection, IDOR,
106:   per-route access control, XSS sinks in individual templates) — these belong to the
107:   `injection` and `access` departments; `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`
108:   (`eval(req.body.preTax)`) and the global `swig.setDefaults({ autoescape: false })`
109:   at `server.js:136-137` were seen while reading but are not reported here as they
110:   are injection findings, not platform-configuration findings.
111: - Third-party dependency vulnerabilities (`package-lock.json`, 888 KB, was not
112:   audited against an advisory database) — that is the `dependencies` department's
113:   scope.
114: - `app/data/*.js` (MongoDB query construction) beyond what was needed to confirm the
115:   error-handling sink.
116: - Static/vendored front-end assets under `app/assets/vendor/` (jQuery, Bootstrap,
117:   Raphael, Morris) were not reviewed for known CVEs in the bundled versions.
118: - Actual deployed runtime configuration: whether a real deployment overrides
119:   `cookieSecret`, sets `NODE_ENV=production` explicitly, or sits behind a
120:   TLS-terminating reverse proxy or WAF that would mask some of the transport
121:   findings above. Nothing in this read-only source tree can confirm or rule that
122:   out; the findings describe what the committed code itself does when run as
123:   written.
124: - CI/CD and GitHub Actions workflows (`.github/workflows/*.yml`) beyond noting that
125:   `semgrep`'s `github-actions-mutable-action-tag` rule fired there; not triaged
126:   further as it is a supply-chain/CI concern rather than a runtime platform
127:   misconfiguration.
128: 
129: ## Certificate
130: 
131: Verified findings: 10/10 resolve to an existing file and line in the locked target
132: tree via `node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/platform.json`
133: (`ok: 10 findings verified against /root/targets/NodeGoat`); all 10 ids are unique;
134: no two findings share `file`, `line` and `cwe` (the two findings that do share a
135: file and line, `platform-session-cookie-not-secure` and
136: `platform-session-cookie-default-name`, carry different CWE ids, CWE-614 and
137: CWE-200, over the same `server.js:78-102` session configuration block).
138: 
139: This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that
140: each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the
141: files listed in "Scope and method".

(End of file - total 141 lines)
</content>

1: # Secrets & leaked configuration — OWASP NodeGoat
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat`, the 111-file tree locked in `target.json` (sha256
6: `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`). This review is a
7: static, line-by-line read by a language model, grounded by Semgrep and by this
8: program's mechanical examiner (`verify-safety-report.mjs`); it is not a dynamic test
9: of a running instance.
10: 
11: `semgrep --version` reported `1.177.0`, so Semgrep ran: `semgrep --config
12: <local code-safety rules> --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json /root/targets/NodeGoat`.
13: The registry pack (`p/owasp-top-ten`) was reachable and loaded 560 community rules
14: alongside 10 custom rules; 113 rules ran over the 72 git-tracked files (36 files were
15: skipped by `.semgrepignore`, mostly vendored front-end assets under
16: `app/assets/vendor/`), producing 29 hits. Every hit was read; the ones from the
17: `dsh-hardcoded-secret` custom rule (`config/env/all.js:8`, `config/env/development.js:6`,
18: `config/env/test.js:6`) are the seed for three of the five findings below. Semgrep's
19: hits were treated strictly as places to read, not as findings on their own — several
20: (the `code-string-concat` and `dsh-eval-on-input` hits on `app/routes/contributions.js`,
21: the mongo-where hits on `app/data/allocations-dao.js`, cookie-setting and open-redirect
22: hits on `server.js`/`app/routes/index.js`) are injection/access-control patterns, not
23: secrets, and are out of scope for this department.
24: 
25: Beyond the scanner, every file the task description names as secret-shaped was read
26: directly: `config/config.js` and all four files under `config/env/`, `server.js`,
27: `app/data/user-dao.js` and `app/data/profile-dao.js`, `artifacts/db-reset.js`,
28: `artifacts/cert/server.key` and `server.crt`, `docker-compose.yml`, `Dockerfile`,
29: `app.json`, `Procfile`, `.travis.yml`, both `.github/workflows/*.yml`, `cypress.json`,
30: `nodemon.json`, `package.json`, `.gitignore`/`.dockerignore`, `test/security/profile-test.js`,
31: and all four fixtures under `test/e2e/fixtures/users/`. Greps were run for
32: `AKIA`, `BEGIN ... PRIVATE KEY`, `mongodb(+srv)?://`, `_auth`/`authToken` in
33: `package-lock.json`, and every name containing `password`, `secret`, `token`, `key`,
34: `credential` or `auth` across the tree. No `.env`, `.npmrc` or `.netrc` file exists in
35: the locked tree (`.gitignore` explicitly excludes `.env`/`.env.local`, and none is
36: present regardless).
37: 
38: ## Findings
39: 
40: Five findings, all `confidence: confirmed` — each is a literal I read at the cited
41: line, traced to how (or whether) the running server actually consumes it.
42: 
43: ### Critical
44: 
45: - **`secrets-cookie-secret`** (`config/env/all.js:8`, CWE-798) — `cookieSecret:
46:   "session_cookie_secret_key_here"` is the literal express-session signs cookies
47:   with. `config/config.js` merges this file under the active environment's config, and
48:   `config/env/production.js` is `module.exports = {};` — it overrides nothing, so this
49:   literal is the live secret in every environment, including a production deploy.
50:   `server.js:82` passes it straight to `session({ secret: cookieSecret, ... })` with no
51:   environment-variable fallback anywhere in the codebase. Anyone who reads this
52:   repository can forge a signed session cookie — including one carrying an admin
53:   `userId` — and walk past every `isLoggedInMiddleware`/`isAdminUserMiddleware` check.
54: 
55: - **`secrets-admin-default-credential`** (`artifacts/db-reset.js:15-20`, CWE-798/CWE-256)
56:   — the database-seeding script (run by `docker-compose.yml`'s startup command and by
57:   `app.json`'s Heroku `postdeploy` hook — not a test fixture) inserts a user
58:   `"userName": "admin"`, `"password": "Admin_123"`, `"isAdmin": true`. `app/data/user-dao.js`
59:   stores passwords verbatim (the bcrypt-hashing line is commented out) and
60:   `validateLogin` compares them with plain `===` (the `bcrypt.compareSync` line is also
61:   commented out). So this is a real, working admin login for any deployment that
62:   follows the documented setup, not a placeholder — it authenticates.
63: 
64: ### Medium
65: 
66: - **`secrets-crypto-key`** (`config/env/all.js:9`, CWE-321) — `cryptoKey:
67:   "a_secure_key_for_crypto_here"`. Its only consumer, the encrypt/decrypt helpers in
68:   `app/data/profile-dao.js`, is entirely commented out, and so are the call sites that
69:   would use it to protect stored SSNs/DOB. As shipped, this key is dead code — stated
70:   here explicitly — but it is still a committed cryptographic key that would silently
71:   become live if that "Fix for A6" block were ever uncommented without rotating it.
72: 
73: - **`secrets-private-key-committed`** (`artifacts/cert/server.key:1-15`, CWE-321/CWE-798)
74:   — a full PEM RSA private key is committed alongside `server.crt`. Its only reference,
75:   the HTTPS server block in `server.js`, is commented out; the server that runs today
76:   is plain HTTP. The key is dead code today but is a real private key in git history
77:   that must be treated as already exposed to anyone with a clone.
78: 
79: ### Low
80: 
81: - **`secrets-zap-api-key`** (`config/env/development.js:6`, also `config/env/test.js:6`,
82:   CWE-798) — `zapApiKey: "v9dn0balpqas1pcc281tn5ood1"` authenticates
83:   `test/security/profile-test.js` to a local OWASP ZAP proxy at the private address
84:   `192.168.56.20:8080` for the project's own DAST regression suite. It never reaches
85:   `server.js` or any application route, so its blast radius is limited to whoever can
86:   already reach that private test-network ZAP instance.
87: 
88: ## What was not covered
89: 
90: - The 36 files Semgrep skipped via `.semgrepignore` were not re-scanned by the tool,
91:   though they were covered by manual grep; they are vendored front-end libraries
92:   (`app/assets/vendor/**`) unlikely to carry project secrets.
93: - Git history was not searched for secrets removed from `HEAD` (no `git log -p`/
94:   gitleaks/trufflehog pass over the full history); this review only certifies what is
95:   in the currently locked tree, and any of the five secrets above may also exist in
96:   earlier commits.
97: - No live/dynamic check was run against a deployed instance; findings about "the
98:   running server" are inferred from reading `server.js`'s active (uncommented) code
99:   path, not from observing a live process.
100: - Non-secrets findings that Semgrep's OWASP-Top-Ten pack surfaced (session-cookie
101:   hardening, open redirect, string-concatenation/eval patterns, NoSQL `$where` usage,
102:   mutable GitHub Action tags, plaintext HTTP links in tutorial pages) were read only
103:   far enough to confirm they are not secrets, and are left for the access/injection/
104:   platform departments.
105: - `package-lock.json` (888 KB) was grep-scanned for registry-auth patterns only, not
106:   read line by line.
107: 
108: ## Certificate
109: 
110: This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that
111: each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the
112: files listed in "Scope and method". Verified with `node verify-safety-report.mjs
113: --findings findings/secrets.json` → `ok: 5 findings verified against
114: /root/targets/NodeGoat`.

(End of file - total 114 lines)
</content>
